On the Macau Strip lies an arena. This arena, the [Cotai Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotai_Arena), has been used for countless events. But it seems it is to be undergoing renovation in the coming months.

Chinese Billionaires [Jack Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ma) and [Robin Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Li) have talked to the owners of the Cotai Arena, and have worked out a purchase of the arena. It is to be closed for the remainder of the year, while construction is happening on the inside.

In a short blog post, Jack Ma notes a few changes that were going to be added to the arena. Some of the major changes were top of the line security systems, [an announcer podium](http://globalmemo.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/UN_General_Assembly_empty.png), blastproof panic rooms stocked with supplies to last for weeks, air purifiers and power generation rooms, and state of the art medical bays. Jack projects the cost of the renovations to be just shy of one billion USD.

Additionally, at the bottom of the post, it seemed that they were to contact several persons of high power around the world. They said it could range from other billionaires, to leaders.

*Klingons first glowered from television screens in 1968. These aggressive warriors were scripted speaking only English until the 1979 release of Star Trek: The Motion Picture, when viewers heard guttural shouts from the crew of a doomed Klingon spaceship. Only the subtitles knew what they were saying: the actors themselves put emotion into what were then meaningless sounds. Then, two Star Trek movies later, the producers called on professional linguist Dr. Marc Okrand to create authentic speech for the Klingons. His task was to make their language as alien as their ridged prosthetic foreheads, while still remaining pronounceable by human actors and consistent with the battle cries from the first movie.

Dr. Okrand did not base Klingon on any particular language, but drew on his knowledge of how language works to construct a wholly new language. During filming, he coached the actors on pronunciation, and then amended Klingon to match not only their mispronunciations, but also changes made to the subtitles after the lines were recorded. Dr. Okrand’s description of the language he created was published in 1985 as The Klingon Dictionary.*

Ferdinand Porsche presents Adolf Hitler with a 50th birthday gift: a convertible Volkswagen Beetle. April 20, 1939.

This is one in a series of photos Hitler's personal photographer, Hugo Jaeger, took during the celebrations on Hitler's 50th birthday. Further photos and information here.

Hugo Jeager took about 2,000 color photos of Hitler. Towards the end of WW2 in 1945, during a search of the house where Jaeger was staying, American soldiers found the leather satchel in which these images were stored. The bag also contained a bottle of brandy and a small, ivory gambling toy—a spinning top for a game of chance known as “put-and-take.” Happy with their find, the soldiers sat down to a session of put-and-take while sharing the bottle of brandy with Jaeger and the owner of the house.

After this scare, Jaeger buried the photographs inside 12 glass jars outside Munich. He returned to the burial site over several years to ensure they were safe. He dug up all of the photographs ten years later in 1955, and stored them in a bank vault until 1965, when he sold them to Life magazine.
